query: What are CPSO requirements for virtual care consent?

match_criteria.reason: Contains CPSO virtual care consent requirements and documentation standards

expected_answer_elements: Explicit consent required for virtual care
Cite: CPSO Policy on Virtual Care
expert_answer: CPSO requires informed consent for virtual care that includes informing patients about: (1) benefits of virtual care, (2) limitations of virtual care, and (3) potential risks including privacy risks, clinical limitations, and potential need for in-person follow-up. Consent must be obtained during the initial virtual encounter and re-obtained if the virtual modality changes or nature of care significantly changes. For less secure technology, physicians must obtain express (verbal or written) consent and document it in the medical record. Physicians must also confirm patient identity, disclose all participants in the encounter, ask if patient is in a private setting, and confirm patient's comfort sharing personal health information. (Cite: CPSO Policy on Virtual Care, June 2022; Advice to the Profession: Virtual Care, June 2022)

query: What medical records must I keep for telemedicine visits?

match_criteria.reason: Contains CPSO medical records requirements for telemedicine

expected_answer_elements: Cite: CPSO Policy on Medical Records
expert_answer: CPSO requires the same comprehensive documentation standards for telemedicine visits as for in-person encounters. Physicians must document: (1) presenting complaint, (2) focused relevant history, (3) assessment and examination, (4) diagnosis/differential diagnosis, (5) treatment/therapy and patient response, and (6) management and follow-up plan. For telephone and electronic communications, physicians must capture details of all communication with patients related to clinical care, including the mode of communication and clinical details. Documentation must be legible, accurate, complete, professionally written, dated, and identifiable by author. Documentation should be completed as soon as possible after the patient encounter. No separate retention periods are specified for virtual encounters - the same general medical records retention requirements apply. (Cite: CPSO Policy on Medical Records Documentation, March 2020)

query: Can I prescribe opioids via virtual care? What are all the requirements?

match_criteria.reason: Contains CPSO opioid prescribing requirements and virtual care limitations

expected_answer_elements: Virtual care prescribing restrictions for opioids
Cite: CPSO Prescribing Drugs policy, Virtual Care policy
expert_answer: CPSO does not explicitly prohibit prescribing opioids via virtual care, but requires careful evaluation. Physicians must: (1) follow the Prescribing Drugs policy which requires an appropriate clinical assessment before prescribing, (2) carefully evaluate whether they can appropriately assess and mitigate the unique risks of opioids (misuse, abuse, diversion) without an in-person assessment, and (3) conduct a risk-benefit analysis to determine if virtual prescribing is appropriate for the specific patient and circumstances. Before prescribing opioids, physicians must: obtain relevant patient history, conduct appropriate examinations (which may be limited virtually), consider if it's the most appropriate choice, document no reasonable alternatives exist, mitigate potential risks, develop a comprehensive treatment plan, review patient's prescription history, and inform patients of risks including dependence and overdose. If a physical examination is required to appropriately assess or treat the patient, virtual care may not meet the standard of care. The physician must use professional judgment to determine when virtual prescribing is suitable. (Cite: CPSO Policy on Virtual Care, June 2022; Advice to the Profession: Virtual Care, June 2022; CPSO Policy on Prescribing Drugs, December 2019)

query: What are CPSO expectations for continuity of care?

match_criteria.reason: Contains CPSO continuity of care expectations and coverage requirements

expected_answer_elements: Cite: CPSO Policy on Continuity of Care
expert_answer: CPSO expects physicians to maintain continuity of care through several requirements: (1) Availability - physicians must have an office phone that allows voicemails during business hours, review and respond to voicemails in a timely manner, respond promptly when contacted by other healthcare providers, and structure their practice to allow timely access to appointments for urgent or time-sensitive issues. (2) Coverage during temporary absences - for planned absences, physicians must make specific coverage arrangements with another healthcare provider for receiving/reviewing outstanding test results and consultation reports, have a communication plan for other providers, and make reasonable efforts to arrange patient care coverage. (3) Patient communication - physicians must inform patients about where to access care outside office hours, specific coverage arrangements during absence, and alternative care options if no specific coverage is arranged. (4) Critical test results - ensure critical test results can be received and reviewed at all times, with a process to notify patients if emergency intervention is required. (Cite: CPSO Policy on Availability and Coverage, September 2019; Advice to the Profession: Continuity of Care)

query: Can I send lab results to patients via email?

match_criteria.reason: Contains CPSO requirements for electronic PHI transmission and patient communication

expected_answer_elements: Encryption requirements for email with PHI
Cite: CPSO Policy on Protecting Personal Health Information
expert_answer: Yes, but CPSO has specific requirements for sending lab results (personal health information/PHI) via email. (1) Encryption requirement - physicians must use encrypted e-communication when communicating PHI to patients, where possible. (2) If encryption is not possible - physicians must obtain patient's express consent after informing the patient about: how e-communication will be used, type of information communicated, how communication will be processed, and limitations and risks of unencrypted communication. (3) Documentation - physicians must obtain and document the patient's express consent to use unencrypted communication, including documenting discussions about communication risks. (4) Considerations when evaluating unencrypted communication - physicians must evaluate: sensitivity of PHI, volume and frequency of communication, purpose of transmission, patient expectations, alternative communication methods, and urgent circumstances. The policy emphasizes using encrypted communication whenever possible, with unencrypted email only used after informed patient consent and careful risk evaluation. (Cite: CPSO Policy on Protecting Personal Health Information, March 2020; Advice to the Profession: Protecting Personal Health Information, January 2023)
